A Life of Terror - The Singwa Namhla Mtwa Story

By: Sophia Phirippides | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
It’s blown up through social media, yet another case of Gender Based Violence and murder gone unnoticed, until now. Why do authorities need community pressure to act?

Unique Selling Point:
We dig deeper behind the Singwa Namhla Mtwa Murder.

Trending on social media and then blowing up on the news, images of horror and terror - a murder and a case of gender based violence that remained uninvestigated by the local police in Mthatha in the EC for over a month. Singwa Namhla Mtwa, 35, was allegedly shot nine times by a man in her driveway in Mthatha on 21 April 2022. She died at the scene. Her sister witnessed the murder and fears for her own life. We take a deeper look into Namhla’s life, as experts look at motive, and profile the possible killer as well as look at why law enforcement has not acted on an obvious suspect.

Summary:
Namhla, as she is known by her family appears to have been in a 17 year abusive relationship with a local business tycoon, Major Mfesane Bhekizulu, who is currently out on R50 000 bail since 2018, for murder and attempted murder of two of his employees.

He says he had nothing to do with Namhla’s death. The police have made no arrests. Videos and photographs released on social media reflect a life of terror and abuse by this man. Yet he’s still not in custody. Based on his bail conditions and on the evidence from photographs and videos, according to experts he should at least already be being questioned or in custody for assault, which would put in jeopardy his bail conditions. So why are local authorities not acting? Who is Major Mfesane Bhekizulu and why does he seem untouchable? We speak to experts and profilers who will give us a breakdown of what kind of suspects should be being looked at and where law enforcement is failing women and especially Namhla Mtwa.

Further information:
Treatment:

Mthatha: A place where allegations of GBV go unattended as a matter of course, there are many accounts on social media of this taking place. We take a deeper look at the town the people and their fears. How they feel about the local authorities, especially the police, we paint a picture of the town and its significance. We speak to Namhla’s family, maybe friends describing her as a person, and then exploring her painful and fear-filled life with Bhekizulu. We take a more Crime and Investigation approach, with expert Lobo Das Neves, dissecting the crime scene and what kind of a perpetrator would perform such an act. He also looks at the bail case of Bhekizulu and why there is a problem with what is going on. We speak to Dr Lesley Ann Foster on GBV and the red flags around this case. The piece will be moody and take on a more crime and investigation feel to it, rather than try and follow the news.

Background information:

We visit the scene of the crime if possible and speak to members of her family.

The bigger issue here is, whether or not Bhekizulu is guilty, her long time partner Major Mfesane, a man accused of murder and with evidence of his brutal relationship with Namhla, why has his bail not been revoked?

A special senior Brigadier Venetia Masingi has now been appointed to investigate the case. This is normally only done in politically motivated murders or the like, why is everyday policing failing ordinary South Africans? The EFF have marched, the local King has give the police 3 days to make an arrest, Minister Bheki Cele was meant to visit the family today, but apparently he has not arrived. He has stated that social media evidence is not enough evidence to make an arrest and proper policing should be conducted. If this is so, then why has it not been done to date? Why has it also taken 4 years to get the murder cases against Bhekizulu to court. All these questions remain unanswered. We attempt to connect and expose this very sinister story.

We speak to law enforcement. The family. Profiler and Police Expert. GBV expert.

Press Release:


It’s blown up through social media, yet another case of Gender Based Violence and murder gone unnoticed, until now. Why do authorities need community pressure to act?

Script:


VO: It’s a busy morning on the streets of Mthatha in the Eastern Cape… But beneath this bustling exterior, is a violent underbelly…


Nomana: he shoved me under the delivery bed. And then that's where he raped me at gunpoint.


VO: A terrifying recollection from Nomana Ntshakaza, a nurse who along with her colleagues, was brutally attacked and raped in this town….
But Nomana’s story isn't what initially brought me here.
[ four gunshots ]
VO: On the 21st of April this year, municipal worker Singwa Namhla Mtwa, fondly nicknamed Hle-Hle, parked in her driveway…
[ five gunshots ]
VO: A gunman emerged from the darkness and shot her nine times… before casually walking away…
Zipo: when Namhla Mtwa was murdered… to the rest of the town, it seemed like just another random killing…. But what was strange to everyone is that the car wasn't stolen. Her cell phone was stolen her none of her belongings were stolen.
VO: A month later, police still did not have suspects. Angry and frustrated, her sister, Sanga took to social media…
Zipo-Zenkosi Ncokazi is a freelance journalist based in Mthatha…


Zipo: Sanga started posting on Facebook “justice for HleHle” because she felt like the police were taking too long, even though there was a suspect or a person of interest. And she started sharing old WhatsApp pictures and old WhatsApp texts between her and Namhla, where Namhla was telling Sanga that she's being abused…


LINK: I was scrolling through social media when Namhla Mtwa’s story went viral and I avoided it, I scrolled past the posts, I didn’t want to engage with the posts… I didn’t feel like I had the emotional capacity to deal with another gender-based violence story… all I kept on thinking was, here we go again South Africa…

VO: Namhla’s story is only the tip of the GBV crisis in this country, but in small towns like Mthatha… it seems it’s a problem that’s often ignored…


Siyamthanda: We are still in the top 30 hotspot areas of GBV. And it's true Mthatha is a hotspot…
VO: Eastern Cape activist Siyamathanda Ndlela says she has seen the worst cases of GBV in her community…
Siyathanda: it's bad. It's actually bad than what the media reports. When you go deep into the rural areas, you'll see a lot of horrible thing when we speak of GBV where there's still rape they're still forced child marriages.

Claire: Are women reporting these cases to the police?
Siya: those cases are underreported, you must remember that in Mthatha is surrounded by many rural areas. And in villages, they still have that mentality of, we discuss the problems which are related to GBV within the family, we go to speak about the rape cases, if the neighbor has raped the neighbor's child, they're gonna come to us and apologize, give us a sheep or goat to slaughter to wash away all the debt. So they don't really report
LINK: When a woman is a victim of gender based violence, where does she go to? The police of course, but we hear the same stories, over and over again, that there is no help, they get ignored or are told to fix the problem at home…


Lobo: While it's disturbing to know that there are obviously some police officers that not not doing the work as they should… there are national instructions that specifically describe a policeman's duty when they become aware of domestic violence Act case….
VO: Lobo das Neves, is a South African police service veteran and law enforcement expert. He also contributed to the drafting of the Domestic Violence Act…
Lobo: The fact that we believe a certain person did something can often be an emotional thing. But it's not proof or evidence. And it's for the authority to now go and collect whatever evidence there is…bring it to a court and see if there are grounds sufficient enough to institute prosecution against the suspect.
VO: With no arrests so far, police are still investigating Namhla’s murder, but communities have run out of patience. In Mthatha protesters gathered to march to the central police station calling for justice…


LINK:
I know that the police and the judicial system play an important critical role in stopping gender based violence. But that doesn't absolve you and I as community members have the responsibility to also fight gender based violence. What are you and I doing? That is the challenge… because in Mthatha, it is the belief system of the communities that allow these perpetrators to continue doing what they're doing.





VO: And it’s clear that, despite years of fighting this scourge, our society is beset by a culture of violence.… which brings us to the story of Nomana Nchakaza, who in 2001, was on night shift at a local clinic….
NOMANA: And as the night progressed, there was no no patients. But all of a sudden, around midnight, we heard noise. And we thought of maybe they are people with emergency…
VO: Instead, Nomana and her colleagues came face to face with two armed men…
NOMANA: they started to pull out guns pointing at us looking for money.. Then from that waiting room where we were … the bossy one started to say to me you must go this side. And then he shoved me with a gun. It was like pointed here a shoved me to the labor wards. And he said we are going to rape you…
Claire: during that time. Did you think that your life was at risk? …
NOMANA: I was waiting for my death… When I started to pray there were no words. You know, when you say O Bawo, O Bawo. Oh, but oh my god. And I realized that, hey, I am wasting time. Let me cite the Lord's Prayer… But when I reached the end, I couldn't say Amen instead, I started all over again, for all those hours until we were rescued.
VO: But Nomana’s ordeal didn’t end there - hours after they were rescued, there were no rape kits available to collect evidence… so for more than 24 hours after being gang raped, a determined Nomana did not bath as she waited for the police…

NOMANA: You expected not to wash not to change anything, you have to preserve the evidence because they have to take the vaginal fluid so that they can get semen…. It's quite not a nice experience… what you are hearing most of the time is the strength of this case depends upon you…
VO: Within six months, both perpetrators were arrested and convicted for her gang rape… a brutal crime that irrevocably changed Nomana’s life forever…
LINK: I don't know what I would do as a woman living in this community. As somebody who was a victim of gender based violence, or just a community member, the resources are not here. The help is not here. And the belief systems here, only fuel gender based violence.


VO: It’s still unclear whether Namhla reported each incident of violence to police but Sanga’s social media posts painted a dark history of physical, psychological and emotional abuse spanning 17 years.
And at the heart of it, were claims that Namhla’s long-term boyfriend and alleged abuser, Major Mfesane Bhekezulu, was responsible for her death…
But this wasn’t the first time that Bhekezulu’s name had come up in a murder investigation…
Zipo:
When I saw Sanga’s posts, Namhla Mtwa’s sister’s posts, I was like, not this guy again with another alleged murder…
Zipo: According to the police reports, the three employees were last seen being picked up by Major Bhekezulu….. And both of them never made it to their homes. The one guy's body was then found the next morning, and the other guy was found in hospital. But he was the last person to be seen with them. And hence, he was the main suspect, and the police arrested him.
VO: In 2018, Bhekezulu appeared in court for the murder and attempted murder of two of his employees.


Zipo: he denied all the charges against him… he admitted that he indeed did pick them up the previous night. But he doesn't know what happened to them. The next day, he was granted 50k bail, and there was nothing ever heard of the case after that….
LINK: President Cyril Ramaphosa once said, and I quote, When a man has been arrested for rape, killing and even assault, they must not be given bail, close quote. But getting bail seems to be quite easy for alleged perpetrators. What's terrifying for the victims is that the accused gets to go home and reenter the same community, and who knows when the case will ever see the light of day.
SIYAMTHANDA: I think we should stop granting them bail. Because the thing of granting them bail also make the community to lose hope, towards the justice system. Because the community doesn't actually understand what it is. They're gonna ask you what is the use of going to report and then the next day he is coming back out, he's granted R400 bail, and then back in the society repeating the same thing.
Lobo: Bail is a process to guarantee an accused presence in court after being released… So it's not about the offense…. It's about the amount of money that the court determines would most likely guarantee the suspects or the accused presents in court with the next hearing date. And that is very poorly understood…
LINK: The thing with gender based violence. South African women live with it daily, even if it is not affecting us directly. We still have to go out there and make a living, go to work, be parents be great partners, be friends, daughters. It lives with us because we are constantly wondering, Am I next? Is that me? That will be marching for next month? Is that going to be me?


VO: Bhekezulu denies all allegations against him. He declined to be interviewed.
Meanwhile survivors of gender based violence like Nomana send a message of hope…
Twenty years after her rape she has written a book for other survivors… and who knows, one day there may be justice for Namhla after all…

VO: And it’s clear that, despite years of fighting this scourge, our society is beset by a culture of violence.… which brings us to the story of Nomana Nchakaza, who in 2001, was on night shift at a local clinic…. NOMANA: And as the night progressed, there was no no patients. But all of a sudden, around midnight, we heard noise. And we thought of maybe they are people with emergency… VO: Instead, Nomana and her colleagues came face to face with two armed men… NOMANA: they started to pull out guns pointing at us looking for money.. Then from that waiting room where we were … the bossy one started to say to me you must go this side. And then he shoved me with a gun. It was like pointed here a shoved me to the labor wards. And he said we are going to rape you… Claire: during that time. Did you think that your life was at risk? … NOMANA: I was waiting for my death… When I started to pray there were no words. You know, when you say O Bawo, O Bawo. Oh, but oh my god. And I realized that, hey, I am wasting time. Let me cite the Lord's Prayer… But when I reached the end, I couldn't say Amen instead, I started all over again, for all those hours until we were rescued. VO: But Nomana’s ordeal didn’t end there - hours after they were rescued, there were no rape kits available to collect evidence… so for more than 24 hours after being gang raped, a determined Nomana did not bath as she waited for the police… NOMANA: You expected not to wash not to change anything, you have to preserve the evidence because they have to take the vaginal fluid so that they can get semen…. It's quite not a nice experience… what you are hearing most of the time is the strength of this case depends upon you… VO: Within six months, both perpetrators were arrested and convicted for her gang rape… a brutal crime that irrevocably changed Nomana’s life forever… LINK: I don't know what I would do as a woman living in this community. As somebody who was a victim of gender based violence, or just a community member, the resources are not here. The help is not here. And the belief systems here, only fuel gender based violence. VO: It’s still unclear whether Namhla reported each incident of violence to police but Sanga’s social media posts painted a dark history of physical, psychological and emotional abuse spanning 17 years. And at the heart of it, were claims that Namhla’s long-term boyfriend and alleged abuser, Major Mfesane Bhekezulu, was responsible for her death… But this wasn’t the first time that Bhekezulu’s name had come up in a murder investigation… Zipo: When I saw Sanga’s posts, Namhla Mtwa’s sister’s posts, I was like, not this guy again with another alleged murder… Zipo: According to the police reports, the three employees were last seen being picked up by Major Bhekezulu….. And both of them never made it to their homes. The one guy's body was then found the next morning, and the other guy was found in hospital. But he was the last person to be seen with them. And hence, he was the main suspect, and the police arrested him. VO: In 2018, Bhekezulu appeared in court for the murder and attempted murder of two of his employees. Zipo: he denied all the charges against him… he admitted that he indeed did pick them up the previous night. But he doesn't know what happened to them. The next day, he was granted 50k bail, and there was nothing ever heard of the case after that…. LINK: President Cyril Ramaphosa once said, and I quote, When a man has been arrested for rape, killing and even assault, they must not be given bail, close quote. But getting bail seems to be quite easy for alleged perpetrators. What's terrifying for the victims is that the accused gets to go home and reenter the same community, and who knows when the case will ever see the light of day. SIYAMTHANDA: I think we should stop granting them bail. Because the thing of granting them bail also make the community to lose hope, towards the justice system. Because the community doesn't actually understand what it is. They're gonna ask you what is the use of going to report and then the next day he is coming back out, he's granted R400 bail, and then back in the society repeating the same thing. Lobo: Bail is a process to guarantee an accused presence in court after being released… So it's not about the offense…. It's about the amount of money that the court determines would most likely guarantee the suspects or the accused presents in court with the next hearing date. And that is very poorly understood… LINK: The thing with gender based violence. South African women live with it daily, even if it is not affecting us directly. We still have to go out there and make a living, go to work, be parents be great partners, be friends, daughters. It lives with us because we are constantly wondering, Am I next? Is that me? That will be marching for next month? Is that going to be me? VO: Bhekezulu denies all allegations against him. He declined to be interviewed. Meanwhile survivors of gender based violence like Nomana send a message of hope… Twenty years after her rape she has written a book for other survivors… and who knows, one day there may be justice for Namhla after all…

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): It’s blown up through social media, yet another case of Gender Based Violence and murder gone unnoticed, until now. Why do authorities need community pressure to act?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: We dig deeper behind the Singwa Namhla Mtwa Murder. Trending on social media and then blowing up on the news, images of horror and terror - a murder and a case of gender based violence that remained uninvestigated by the local police in Mthatha in the EC for over a month. Singwa Namhla Mtwa, 35, was allegedly shot nine times by a man in her driveway in Mthatha on 21 April 2022. She died at the scene. Her sister witnessed the murder and fears for her own life. We take a deeper look into Namhla’s life, as experts look at motive, and profile the possible killer as well as look at why law enforcement has not acted on an obvious suspect.
metadata.Summary: Namhla, as she is known by her family appears to have been in a 17 year abusive relationship with a local business tycoon, Major Mfesane Bhekizulu, who is currently out on R50 000 bail since 2018, for murder and attempted murder of two of his employees. He says he had nothing to do with Namhla’s death. The police have made no arrests. Videos and photographs released on social media reflect a life of terror and abuse by this man. Yet he’s still not in custody. Based on his bail conditions and on the evidence from photographs and videos, according to experts he should at least already be being questioned or in custody for assault, which would put in jeopardy his bail conditions. So why are local authorities not acting? Who is Major Mfesane Bhekizulu and why does he seem untouchable? We speak to experts and profilers who will give us a breakdown of what kind of suspects should be being looked at and where law enforcement is failing women and especially Namhla Mtwa.
metadata.Further information: Treatment: Mthatha: A place where allegations of GBV go unattended as a matter of course, there are many accounts on social media of this taking place. We take a deeper look at the town the people and their fears. How they feel about the local authorities, especially the police, we paint a picture of the town and its significance. We speak to Namhla’s family, maybe friends describing her as a person, and then exploring her painful and fear-filled life with Bhekizulu. We take a more Crime and Investigation approach, with expert Lobo Das Neves, dissecting the crime scene and what kind of a perpetrator would perform such an act. He also looks at the bail case of Bhekizulu and why there is a problem with what is going on. We speak to Dr Lesley Ann Foster on GBV and the red flags around this case. The piece will be moody and take on a more crime and investigation feel to it, rather than try and follow the news. Background information: We visit the scene of the crime if possible and speak to members of her family. The bigger issue here is, whether or not Bhekizulu is guilty, her long time partner Major Mfesane, a man accused of murder and with evidence of his brutal relationship with Namhla, why has his bail not been revoked? A special senior Brigadier Venetia Masingi has now been appointed to investigate the case. This is normally only done in politically motivated murders or the like, why is everyday policing failing ordinary South Africans? The EFF have marched, the local King has give the police 3 days to make an arrest, Minister Bheki Cele was meant to visit the family today, but apparently he has not arrived. He has stated that social media evidence is not enough evidence to make an arrest and proper policing should be conducted. If this is so, then why has it not been done to date? Why has it also taken 4 years to get the murder cases against Bhekizulu to court. All these questions remain unanswered. We attempt to connect and expose this very sinister story. We speak to law enforcement. The family. Profiler and Police Expert. GBV expert.
